evals.name: scan-helpdesk-repo
evals.prompt: Take a look at the helpdesk service in evals/fixtures/helpdesk. We're evaluating TypeSafe's Jev model. Where in this codebase would it make sense to use it, and where would it be a mistake? Give me a written recommendation I can forward to the team.
evals.expected_output: A report listing candidates with verdicts. Team assignment, urgency, refund detection, frustration score, moderation flags, and KB reranking should be identified as candidates (USE / USE WITH GUARDS / PILOT FIRST). SLA breach, days-since-payment, is_overdue, draft_reply, and the invoice extraction as a whole should be called out as non-candidates (arithmetic/date logic, generation, open extraction) with a note that invoice extraction could become verification-by-Jev of an LLM extraction, and the duplicate check could become a Noul per candidate pair. Economics should compare against the incumbent gpt-5-mini calls at the stated volumes, mention the 120k posts/day moderation volume against rate limits, and cite dated facts.
expectations: Identifies frustration_score, moderation needs_review, and assign_team as Jev candidates
Marks sla_breached, days_since_last_payment, and is_overdue as non-candidates because of date/arithmetic logic
Marks draft_reply as a non-candidate because it generates text
Keeps invoice extraction with an LLM and gives Jev a concrete role behind it (per-field verifier Nouls or selection among regex candidates), not a throwaway single 'is this ok' check
Suggests a reranking step for top_k_articles using one question per candidate, not all candidates packed into one state
Recommends an explicit none/other option or an existence Noul for the team classification
Gives a cost estimate for at least one candidate using volumes stated in the code (20k tickets/day, 120k posts/day)
Compares Jev's cost against a cheap same-tier LLM (e.g. Gemini Flash-Lite, GLM/Qwen/DeepSeek Flash), not only against the incumbent gpt-5-mini or a frontier model
Flags at least one yellow-signal guard (adversarial forum content, non-English, thresholds, vendor risk) with a mitigation
Gives each candidate an explicit graded verdict that distinguishes unconditional use from use-with-guards from pilot-first from no (not just 'replace' / 'keep')
States that quoted prices/limits are dated and names where to re-check them
Proposes a pilot with real labelled samples before automation for at least one candidate
Keeps the BANNED word list in code ahead of Jev and proposes per-category thresholds for the moderation flags
Bounds the reranking design: caps the shortlist size and checks concurrency or rate-limit headroom at 20k tickets/day
Gives both per-day and per-month cost figures and they are consistent with each other and with the stated tokens, volume and $0.042/M

Proposes at least two new capabilities that do not exist in the code (e.g. plain-language ticket filters for agents, live frustration meter while an agent types, per-row scoring of the ticket archive, verifying draft_reply against the KB), labelled as new capabilities
The summary's verdict counts and candidate list match the body (no candidate or proposal missing from the tally, no list duplicated)

evals.name: single-decision-polish-classifier
evals.prompt: We run a Polish-language e-commerce marketplace. Sellers upload product listings (title + description in Polish) and today a rules engine plus a manual queue decides whether a listing is prohibited (weapons, counterfeit, medicine). ~40k new listings per day, moderators handle ~6k of them manually. A colleague suggests switching the first pass to TypeSafe's Jev. Should we? Be concrete about accuracy, cost, speed, and what we'd have to test before trusting it.
evals.expected_output: A verdict of PILOT FIRST (or USE WITH GUARDS conditioned on a pilot), explicitly because the input is Polish and no Polish evaluation exists; a sketch with one Noul per prohibited category plus a severity Score and a review band; a cost estimate for 40k listings/day from measured or assumed token counts; a note about adversarial sellers wording listings to evade detection and Jev not being a security boundary on its own; a comparison with alternatives (fine-tuned multilingual encoder on the existing moderation labels, cheap multilingual LLM); a pilot design with a few hundred labelled listings and probe.py-style metrics.
expectations: Verdict is PILOT FIRST or explicitly conditional on a pilot, citing Polish-language uncertainty
States that TypeSafe documents English as the primary training language with lower accuracy for other languages
States that no evaluation of Jev on real (non-synthetic) Polish text is known, at most a small synthetic pilot

Decomposes the judgment into per-category questions (one Noul per prohibited category, optionally plus a Choice with a none/allowed option) rather than a single multi-way Choice or one broad 'is this prohibited' question
Recommends a review band / thresholds that route uncertain listings to moderators instead of auto-blocking
Warns that adversarial sellers can steer the model and recommends Jev not be the sole gate
Provides a cost estimate for ~40k listings/day with stated token assumptions
Mentions the existing manual-queue labels as training data for a fine-tuned multilingual classifier alternative
Specifies a pilot: sample size, labels, metrics (agreement, uncertain band share, repeat stability, latency)
Does not claim Jev is hallucination-free or always correct because outputs are typed
Keeps the existing rules engine as an independent signal or floor rather than replacing it outright
Gives a cost table from the skill's script or explicit arithmetic that includes at least one same-tier LLM rival per item, not only Jev's own cost
States a numeric pass bar for the pilot (e.g. minimum agreement, maximum uncertain-band share, latency)

evals.name: cost-comparison-vs-cheap-llm
evals.prompt: Quick question: we classify ~300k customer emails a day into 12 intents with DeepSeek in JSON mode, roughly 700 input tokens and 30 output tokens per email, about 1.5-2.5 s latency. Someone says Jev would be 400x cheaper. Is that true for us, and would it be as accurate?
evals.expected_output: A grounded answer: the 400x figure is TypeSafe's self-tested peak against frontier models, not against DeepSeek-class pricing; an actual per-day/per-month comparison using DeepSeek's current price and Jev's $0.042/M input with the given token counts (Jev should come out cheaper but by a much smaller multiple, roughly single-digit to low double-digit); accuracy framed as 'same tier as mid-range LLMs, decomposition and an other option matter, pilot on 200 emails'; latency ~100-500 ms vs 1.5-2.5 s; rate-limit check for 300k/day (~3.5 req/s average, peak may approach limits); a note that Choice over 12 intents with an other option and confidence gating is the shape.
expectations: Says the 400x claim is vendor-reported and measured against frontier models, not DeepSeek-class pricing
Computes a per-day or per-month cost for Jev at 300k emails/day that counts the question and option tokens on top of the ~700-token email
Computes the DeepSeek cost with a stated current price per million tokens (and dates it)
Reports a realistic cost ratio much lower than 400x
Addresses accuracy as comparable to a mid-tier LLM with a recommendation to pilot on labelled emails
Recommends a Choice over the 12 intents with an other/none option and confidence gating
Checks the workload against the published rate limits (40 req/s, 100k tokens/s as of 2026-10-01)
Notes latency improvement from seconds to sub-second and asks whether it matters for the workflow
Recommends enabling DeepSeek prompt caching (or low reasoning) as a zero-risk first step, since it shrinks the gap

evals.name: greenfield-product-opportunities
evals.prompt: We're building a community platform for board-game players: forum threads, event listings, a marketplace for used games, and a Discord-like live chat. Node/TypeScript backend, Postgres. Where could TypeSafe's Jev add features that would be hard to build otherwise? Give me a shortlist with what each would cost at ~50k chat messages, ~3k forum posts and ~500 listings per day, and which ones you would pilot first.
evals.expected_output: An opportunity-driven shortlist (not a replacement audit): e.g. live chat moderation per message with confidence bands, plain-language feed/notification rules users write themselves, event-to-user interest matching, marketplace listing checks (prohibited/scam/mispriced with price math in code), duplicate listing detection per pair, forum thread quality/answered-question scoring stored as columns, semantic search over threads without embeddings, feature extraction for a recommendation model. Each with question sketch, cost from the stated volumes, guards (adversarial chat, non-English), and a pilot order.
expectations: Presents proposals as new capabilities organised by what they enable, not as replacements of existing code
Includes a real-time per-message chat judgment with a review band or confidence gating
Includes a plain-language rule or personalisation feature where user text goes into the question instructions
Any duplicate/matching design puts both records in the state and judges one pair per request (not several candidates packed into the question text), and keeps price comparisons in code
Persists per-item judgments (forum posts or listings) as queryable columns or a decisions table that other features reuse
Gives a cost estimate per feature from the stated volumes (50k messages, 3k posts, 500 listings per day) using $0.042 per M input tokens
Checks the 50k messages/day chat load against the published rate limits or notes it is far below them
Warns that adversarial chat content can steer Jev and that it should not be the only gate
Recommends a pilot order with a reason for what goes first
Cites at least one named community example or measured number from the use-case catalog or evidence file
The shortlist's total cost matches the sum of the per-feature lines
